items.title: 8 feared killed in Kogi community reprisal attack
items.description: By Boluwaji Obahopo ‎ ‎Several people have been reported killed in a reprisal attack that followed the alleged killing of an unarmed herder by a local vigilante in Kupa Kingdom, Lokoja Local Government Area of Kogi State. ‎ ‎While the actual figures are yet to be ascertained by security agencies, locals report that 8 persons were killed on Wednesday. ‎ ‎The killings occurred in Abugi, Kuchinda and Mikugi communities, where tension reportedly heightened following the death of the herder, who was allegedly shot by a member of the local vigilante on suspicion of cattle rustling. ‎ ‎The subsequent reprisal attack allegedly carried out by armed persons reportedly targeted residents of the three communities, resulting in multiple deaths ‎ ‎The Kogi State Government, while confirming the incidents, described the killings as tragic, senseless and unacceptable, assuring families of the victims that those responsible would be arrested and prosecuted. ‎ ‎In a statement issued on Thursday by the Commissioner for Information and Communications, Kingsley Femi Fanwo, the government said the reprisal attack followed the killing of the herder and had further escalated tension across the affected communities. ‎ ‎Fanwo said Governor Ahmed Ododo had directed security agencies to take immediate control of the situation, restore peace and prevent further attacks. ‎ ‎”The governor has also ordered the arrest of the local vigilante member alleged to have killed the herder, as well as those allegedly responsible for the reprisal attack. ‎ ‎”The leader of the Hybrid Vigilante Group, who was allegedly suspected of coordinating the reprisal assault, is also being sought for arrest.” ‎ ‎Fanwo said the government condemned both the killing of the herder and the subsequent reprisal attack, stressing that neither incident could be justified. ‎ ‎“The Kogi State Government condemns in the strongest terms both the killing of the unarmed herder and the subsequent reprisal attack. These are criminal acts that have no place in our society,” he said. ‎ ‎The commissioner added that anyone found to have participated in either incident, irrespective of status or ethnic affiliation, would face the full weight of the law. ‎ ‎He appealed to residents of Kupa Kingdom to remain calm and avoid further reprisals, urging them to provide credible information to security agencies to assist the ongoing investigation. ‎ ‎Fanwo said the state government was working with security agencies, traditional rulers, community leaders and other stakeholders to restore lasting peace in the affected communities. ‎ ‎He also conveyed the governor’s condolences to the families of those killed, saying Ododo prayed for the repose of the deceased and comfort for their bereaved families. ‎ ‎The commissioner reiterated the administration’s commitment to protecting residents across the state and ensuring that those responsible for the violence were brought to justice. The post 8 feared killed in Kogi community reprisal attack appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Yaadga : Les enjeux et défis du développement au centre de la Journée régionale de concertation
items.description: Yaadga : Les enjeux et défis du développement au centre de la Journée régionale de concertation Ouahigouya, 7 août 2026 (AIB) – Le Gouverneur de la région du Yaadga, Thomas Yampa, a présidé le jeudi 6 août la Journée régionale de concertation (JRC) en présence de plusieurs acteurs du développement de la région, a constaté l'AIB. Cette rencontre a été placée sous le thème « Coordination et synergie d’action des organisations non gouvernementales, associations de développement et fondations dans la région du Yaadga : état des lieux et perspectives ». « C’est une initiative gouvernementale dont l’objectif majeur est d’échanger et d’ouvrir un dialogue direct avec les partenaires au développement qui agissent au quotidien auprès des services déconcentrés de l’État, pour parvenir à un développement harmonieux et inclusif au Burkina Faso », a indiqué le Gouverneur Thomas Yampa. Selon l’autorité régionale, la région du Yaadga compte 361 associations, ONG de développement et fondations qui interviennent dans des domaines importants de l’action de l’État et de ses partenaires. « Cette journée de concertation vise à créer une synergie d’actions autour des différentes réformes majeures afin que chaque acteur, dans son domaine d’intervention, puisse s’aligner dans la dynamique de la Révolution progressiste populaire », a-t-il poursuivi. Le Gouverneur a invité les différents acteurs à plus de dynamisme, d’alignement et de concertation. «Afin que nous puissions faire de ce contexte actuel une situation qui nous amène vers un développement endogène, inclusif et cadré sur les réalités et les valeurs fondamentales de notre Pays », a-t-il ajouté. Au cours de cette journée, trois communications étaient à l’ordre du jour. Le Directeur régional de l’économie et de la planification du Yaadga, Polycarpe Naré a indiqué qu'elles portent sur la résilience et la contribution des ONG, associations et fondations face aux défis dans la région, les innovations majeures de la loi n°011-2025/ALT du 17 juillet 2025 portant liberté d’association et les mécanismes de coordination existants dans la région. Pour le représentant des associations et fondations et des Organisations non gouvernementales (ONG), Adama Ouédraogo, cette journée était très attendue. « Elle va nous permettre d’échanger avec l’autorité et de faire des recommandations pour réussir dans les actions des associations, des fondations et des ONG. Le fait d’avoir un dialogue direct avec l’autorité va nous permettre d’exposer nos préoccupations et de trouver ensemble des solutions idoines », a-t-il déclaré. Il a invité les associations et ONG à se référer au « Plan Relance 2026-2030 », sollicité par le Gouverneur, qui constitue le référentiel du gouvernement en matière de développement. Instituée par décret du gouvernement le 27 mai 2024, la JRC est un cadre de concertation entre l’État, les collectivités territoriales et les acteurs de la société civile. Elle vise à fédérer les actions en faveur du développement local. Agence d’Information du Burkina LG/PN/AS/ATA

items.title: US to vet social media of foreign journalists applying for visas, report says
items.description: The US State Department will ​vet the social media accounts of foreign journalists applying for visas to work in the United ‌States, according to a media report on Thursday. The report in the conservative news outlet The Daily Signal cited an internal memo that said an initiative by President Donald Trump’s administration that requires applicants for many visa types to make their social media accounts public ​for screening was being expanded to include foreign media representatives. Applicants for another type of visa for ​workers from Canada and Mexico also will now be included in the screening, it said. The ⁠White House and the State Department’s official accounts on X shared a link to the article, but the ​State Department declined to confirm the specifics of the report, citing a policy of not commenting on “purported internal documents”. A ​State Department spokesperson said that what the department calls “online presence vetting” is used to ensure that applicants are eligible for a visa under US law. “The Department of State is screening and vetting to the maximum extent possible every foreign national seeking admission to ​the United States to ensure they will respect US law including the terms of their admission and do ​not pose a threat to US security, public safety or national interests,” the spokesperson said. “Officers use a variety of methods to ‌make ⁠informed decisions that protect national security, prevent fraud and ensure a thorough review of applicants,” the spokesperson added. It was unclear when the reported new policy would take effect. The Department of Homeland Security tightened rules last month around how long foreign journalists working in the United States, as well as other visa holders including foreign students, could remain in ​the country. It also builds ​on a series of ⁠ steps that Trump’s administration has taken since he began his second term in taking office in January 2025 to make online speech a factor in immigration and visa decisions. ​These steps have raised concerns among civil liberties advocates about freedom of speech. US Citizenship ​and Immigration Services ⁠has said it will screen the social media posts of immigrants and visa applicants, including for what it deems antisemitic content and “ anti-Americanism ”. The administration has canceled the visas of foreign students in the US who engaged in pro-Palestinian activism, ⁠in some cases attempting to ​deport those students. The State Department said in October 2025 that it ​revoked the visas of six foreign nationals over comments about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk , and said it would continue identifying visa ​holders it believed had celebrated the killing.

Pourtant, rien ne semble pouvoir retarder le départ. Le cortège du Camarade Ministre de la Famille et de la Solidarité, le Lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie KABORÉ, 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗱𝗲 𝗞𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗼𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶, 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗶è𝗿𝗲 é𝘁𝗮𝗽𝗲 𝗱'𝘂𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗮𝗰𝗿é𝗲 𝗮𝘂𝘅 𝘃𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻és 𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝘂 𝗕𝗮𝗺 𝗲𝘁 𝗱𝘂 𝗬𝗮𝗮𝗱𝗴𝗮. Au fil des kilomètres, la pluie accompagne par intermittence la délégation. Les paysages verdoyants témoignent d'une saison agricole bien installée. Ici et là, des cultivateurs sont déjà à l'œuvre dans leurs champs, malgré un ciel toujours menaçant. Vers 8 h 30, le cortège entre dans Kongoussi. Direction le Haut-Commissariat, où un bref échange avec les autorités administratives permet de faire le point sur le déroulement de la mission, les conditions d'accès aux villages et la situation des populations revenues dans leurs localités d'origine. Le briefing achevé, chacun rejoint son véhicule. Cette fois, cap sur le premier village. 9 h 24 le cortège quitte Kongoussi en direction des villages retournés du Bam et du Yaadga. Trois villages sont au programme. Trois étapes. Trois histoires différentes. 𝗠𝗮𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝗻 𝗺ê𝗺𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 : 𝗰𝗲𝗹𝘂𝗶 𝗱𝘂 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗼𝘂𝗿, 𝗱𝗲 𝗹'𝗲𝘀𝗽é𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝘁 𝗱𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. À mesure que nous avançons, les collines dessinent l'horizon. De part et d'autre de la route, quelques cultivateurs travaillent déjà leurs champs pendant que d'autres rejoignent leurs exploitations. Puis la pluie décide de nous accompagner. Au début discrète, elle devient plus insistante. La route rouge se transforme progressivement en un immense miroir d'eau. Par endroits, il devient difficile de distinguer les limites de la chaussée. Les chauffeurs ralentissent. Le cortège avance désormais au pas. Personne ne se plaint. Tous savent que les populations empruntent quotidiennement cette même route. Les kilomètres paraissent interminables. 𝗣𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗽𝗹𝘂𝘀 𝗱𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘂𝘅 𝗵𝗲𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗹𝗮 𝗽𝗹𝘂𝗶𝗲, 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀 𝗱'𝗲𝗮𝘂 𝗲𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗻𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗲. Puis enfin… À 11 h 34, apparaît Komsoré, nom d’emprunt. Sous une pluie persistante, les populations sont là. Elles n'ont pas quitté la place. Femmes, hommes, anciens et jeunes attendent depuis plusieurs heures. Premier arrêt. Premier geste. Comme le veut la tradition, le Camarade Ministre se rend d'abord chez le chef du village pour lui présenter ses civilités et recueillir ses bénédictions. Quelques instants plus tard, les échanges se poursuivent avec les populations. Ce sont les femmes qui prennent la parole. 𝗟𝗲𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝗽𝗿é𝗼𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 à 𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗯𝗿𝗲𝘂𝘅 𝘃𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻é𝘀. Une école fermée depuis plusieurs années. Un CSPS construit depuis seize ans mais jamais fonctionnel. Le besoin d'eau. Des activités génératrices de revenus. Le renforcement de la sécurité. Pendant qu'elles parlent, la pluie finit par s'arrêter. Comme si le ciel lui-même voulait écouter. Le Camarade Ministre transmet alors le message des plus hautes autorités. « 𝙇𝙚 𝙋𝙧𝙚́𝙨𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙙𝙪 𝙁𝙖𝙨𝙤, 𝙡𝙚 𝘾𝙖𝙥𝙞𝙩𝙖𝙞𝙣𝙚 𝙄𝙗𝙧𝙖𝙝𝙞𝙢 𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙤𝙧é 𝙢'𝙖 𝙙𝙚𝙢𝙖𝙣𝙙é 𝙙𝙚 𝙫𝙤𝙪𝙨 𝙙𝙞𝙧𝙚 𝙢𝙚𝙧𝙘𝙞. 𝙈𝙚𝙧𝙘𝙞 𝙙'𝙖𝙫𝙤𝙞𝙧 𝙘𝙝𝙤𝙞𝙨𝙞 𝙙𝙚 𝙧𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙞𝙧 𝙨𝙪𝙧 𝙫𝙤𝙨 𝙩𝙚𝙧𝙧𝙚𝙨. 𝙇𝙚 𝙂𝙤𝙪𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙧𝙖 à 𝙫𝙤𝙨 𝙘ô𝙩é𝙨 𝙥𝙤𝙪𝙧 𝙖𝙘𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙥𝙖𝙜𝙣𝙚𝙧 𝙫𝙤𝙩𝙧𝙚 𝙧𝙚𝙡è𝙫𝙚𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩. » Des paroles simples. Mais qui semblent réchauffer les cœurs. 𝗔𝗽𝗿è𝘀 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗱𝗲 𝘃𝗶𝘃𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝘁 𝗱𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘁é𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗱𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗹è𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗿𝘁è𝗴𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲. À 12 h 46, nous sommes toujours dans les villages du Yatenga. Bienvenue à Farisso, dans le Yaadga. L'accueil est tout aussi chaleureux. Les populations veulent entendre la voix de Ouagadougou. Elles veulent surtout faire entendre la leur. Ici encore, les femmes ouvrent les échanges. Les préoccupations restent les mêmes : l'école, l'eau, les activités économiques, les infrastructures sociales. Le Camarade Ministre écoute longuement. Elle explique que le Gouvernement entend faire du retour des populations une véritable étape de développement. « 𝙄𝙡 𝙣𝙚 𝙨'𝙖𝙜𝙞𝙩 𝙥𝙖𝙨 𝙨𝙚𝙪𝙡𝙚𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙙'𝙖𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙧 𝙡𝙚𝙨 𝙥𝙤𝙥𝙪𝙡𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 à 𝙧𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙞𝙧. 𝙄𝙡 𝙛𝙖𝙪𝙩 𝙘𝙧é𝙚𝙧 𝙡𝙚𝙨 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙙𝙞𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 𝙥𝙤𝙪𝙧 𝙦𝙪'𝙚𝙡𝙡𝙚𝙨 𝙥𝙪𝙞𝙨𝙨𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙫𝙞𝙫𝙧𝙚, 𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙙𝙪𝙞𝙧𝙚 𝙚𝙩 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙨𝙩𝙧𝙪𝙞𝙧𝙚 𝙙𝙪𝙧𝙖𝙗𝙡𝙚𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙡𝙚𝙪𝙧 𝙖𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙞𝙧 𝙞𝙘𝙞 », insiste-t-elle. Elle invite également les communautés à préserver la cohésion sociale, à soutenir les Forces de défense et de sécurité ainsi que les Volontaires pour la Défense de la Patrie et à poursuivre leurs efforts pour reconstruire leurs villages. 14h 28 Changement de région. Le dernier arrêt conduit la délégation à Zamoulou, à une dizaine de kilomètres de Farisso. La scène est désormais familière. Le chef du village accueille la délégation. Les femmes remercient les autorités avant de présenter leurs préoccupations. Les besoins portent essentiellement sur l'accès à l'eau, la réouverture des écoles, les aménagements agricoles et les activités génératrices de revenus. 𝗟𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗲𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗱𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗹é𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲. 𝗘𝗹𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗿é𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗺é𝗱𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗹è𝘃𝗲 𝗱𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗱é𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗲𝘁 𝘀'𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗴𝗲 à 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗺𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗿é𝗼𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝘂𝘅 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁è𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽é𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀. Comme dans les villages précédents, des vivres et du matériel de relèvement sont remis aux populations afin de soutenir leur réinstallation. À 16 h 20, le cortège reprend la route vers Kongoussi. La pluie a laissé place à une route cabossée. La journée semble toucher à sa fin. Du moins, le pensions-nous. Soudain… Le véhicule du Camarade Ministre ralentit. Puis s'immobilise. Les regards se croisent. Personne ne comprend. 𝗟𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝘂 𝘃é𝗵𝗶𝗰𝘂𝗹𝗲 𝗲𝘁 𝘀𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗲 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘂𝗻 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗺𝗽 𝗼ù 𝘂𝗻𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗺𝗺𝗲, 𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗞𝗼𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝘂𝗺𝗼𝘂, 𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝗻 𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗶𝗻 𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗿. Surprise, celle-ci s'arrête de travailler. Le Camarade Ministre lui adresse quelques mots d'encouragement, saisit l'outil de labour et esquisse elle-même quelques sillons. Les applaudissements fusent. Les rires remplacent la fatigue. Quelques mètres plus loin, elle échange avec d'autres producteurs sur le déroulement de la campagne agricole. Elle les encourage à persévérer. Elle leur rappelle que leur retour sur leurs terres constitue déjà une victoire. Et que le Gouvernement continuera à les accompagner pour consolider cette renaissance. Le soleil décline doucement lorsque nous retrouvons Kongoussi. Dans les véhicules, chacun repense aux images de cette journée. Des routes difficiles. Des villages qui reprennent vie. Des femmes debout malgré les épreuves. Des champs de nouveau cultivés. items.title: Benue residents hail Tinubu’s infrastructure drive, pledge support in 2027
items.description: …As Presidential Media Team inspects projects By Soni Daniel Makurdi: The Presidential Media Team, in collaboration with the Renewed Hope Ambassadors has inspected key Federal and Benue State governments’ infrastructure projects across the state, where residents commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration for expanding connectivity through strategic road and bridge projects. The inspection covered the ongoing Buruku-Logo Bridge, the Wurukum Overhead Bridge in Makurdi, the 22-kilometre Makurdi-Gboko Road, and major state infrastructure projects, including the completed High-Level Roundabout Interchange in Makurdi and the Gboko Underpass and Interchange. The Makurdi-Gboko Road forms part of Phase II of the Abuja-Keffi-Akwanga-Lafia-Makurdi Expressway, a strategic corridor linking North Central Nigeria with the South-East. It is expected to be completed by December 2027. The Renewed Hope Ambassadors’ National Media Tour, which has over 40 editors and journalists in the delegation, is designed to independently assess, document and showcase the implementation and impact of key Federal and State governments’ projects under President Tinubu’s administration. A statement by the RHA Director of Media and Publiciry, Tunde Rahman, said the delegation was led by the Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy, Mr. Bayo Onanuga. Speaking during the inspection, Onanuga said the Buruku-Logo Bridge is one of five Federal Government bridges under construction in Benue State and demonstrates the administration’s commitment to investing borrowed funds in productive infrastructure. He said the project would reconnect previously isolated communities, reduce travel time, improve access to markets for farmers and strengthen economic integration across Benue, Taraba and Adamawa states. According to him, the projects are being financed through the Renewed Hope Infrastructure Development Fund, assuring that funding remains adequate for timely completion. “This bridge in particular is the fifth bridge the Federal Government is building in Benue State. I think as Nigerians you see that the government has been accused of so many things including taking loans. You can now see where the money is going. It is to develop infrastructure, to link people who have been forgotten before, to make sure that at least commerce flows freely. “Farmers can get their products straight to the market, they can shorten the travel time between one community and the other, especially between the rural areas and the capital. You can see that this one where we are now, the one in Buruku is going to affect three states, Taraba, Adamawa and to link all of them together to Benue and of course it means to Nigeria,” Onanuga said. The team also inspected the ongoing 25.6-kilometre Captain Dan Road from Lubona Junction to the Tor Tiv Palace, the Food Basket Brewery Limited in Makurdi, and the Federal Government-funded rehabilitation of the Buruku-Gboko Water Treatment Plant at Ameladu Headworks, one of the state’s largest water infrastructure projects. A major highlight of the tour was the inspection of the 1,754-metre Buruku-Logo Bridge. The project links agrarian communities across the River Benue, provides access to neighbouring Taraba State and is expected to boost agriculture, commerce and regional integration. The contractor also employs more than 50 workers from the host community. Residents expressed appreciation to President Tinubu for prioritising infrastructure that addresses longstanding transportation challenges. They described the bridge as a life-saving intervention that would end years of dangerous river crossings and improve the livelihoods of surrounding communities. They also expect the bridge, on completion, to eliminate frequent boat accidents experienced during the rainy season while creating employment opportunities for local youths engaged on the project. Many residents also pledged continued support for President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda, saying the visible impact of ongoing projects had renewed public confidence in the Federal Government. Speaking with journalists, the Deputy Governor of Benue State, Dr Samuel Ode, said the state remained grateful for the Federal Government’s infrastructure investments and expressed confidence that the people would strongly support President Tinubu’s re-election in 2027. He described the ongoing Wurukum Overhead Bridge as a critical intervention on the Abuja-Lafia-Makurdi-Enugu corridor, noting that the junction had for years been notorious for severe traffic congestion, particularly during festive periods. According to him, President Tinubu approved the project following a request by Governor Hyacinth Alia, and construction is progressing rapidly. The Deputy Governor also highlighted the state government’s investment in the Makurdi Central Interchange and Underpass, describing it as a transformative project that connects key routes linking Government House, the Central Business District, Wurukum and the Abuja-Enugu highway, while significantly improving traffic flow within the state capital. “Actually, this road serves as the gateway between the north of the country and the south. Before now we used to have a heavy gridlock here especially during festivities, so the governor of Benue State approached Mr. President for us to have an overhead bridge here. “The President in his magnanimity, graciously approved the construction of this overhead bridge. So work has commenced, moving at a very high speed and the people of Benue are happy because we used to experience quite a lot of difficulties at this point.” The post Benue residents hail Tinubu’s infrastructure drive, pledge support in 2027 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: List of countries in Europe that won’t participate in 2030 World Cup qualifiers
items.description: Only two European countries will be absent from the 2030 FIFA World Cup qualifying campaign after securing automatic places in the tournament as co-hosts. The two nations are Spain and Portugal, who will stage the 2030 World Cup alongside Morocco. FIFA has confirmed that the three main hosts — Spain, Portugal and Morocco — will qualify automatically for the tournament. Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will also receive automatic qualification because they will host the opening matches as part of the centenary celebrations of the first World Cup. Spain Spain will not have to go through the UEFA qualifying process for the 2030 World Cup. The country is one of the three main hosts of the tournament and will stage a large portion of the competition, alongside Portugal and Morocco. As a result, Spain’s place at the 2030 finals is already secured, meaning the national team will not compete for a qualifying spot. Portugal Portugal is the second European country guaranteed a place at the 2030 World Cup without going through qualifiers. The country will co-host the tournament with Spain and Morocco, giving the Portuguese national team automatic qualification. Portugal will therefore be absent from the European qualifying race, although it will still be one of the teams competing at the finals in 2030. Why Spain and Portugal are not in the qualifiers The decision is linked to their status as hosts. FIFA traditionally grants automatic qualification to World Cup hosts, allowing them to take part in the tournament without having to earn their place through qualifying matches. For 2030, the arrangement is unusual because six countries will benefit from automatic qualification. Spain, Portugal and Morocco are the main tournament hosts, while Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will stage the three centenary matches marking 100 years since the inaugural World Cup in Uruguay in 1930. Full list of European countries not participating in 2030 World Cup qualifiers Spain – Automatic qualification as a main host Portugal – Automatic qualification as a main host The remaining European national teams will have to compete for their places through the UEFA qualification process. UEFA has already announced plans for a new qualifying format for the 2030 World Cup, with the European qualification system set to move towards a Champions League-style structure. With Spain and Portugal already guaranteed places, the qualifying campaign will therefore have fewer European teams competing for the available World Cup berths. The 2030 World Cup will be played across Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay hosting the three opening centenary fixtures. items.title: I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil says
items.description: On Friday morning, as the final classes of the week were under way, panicked students began streaming out of a prestigious school just outside Bangkok. Inside, police say, a 14-year-old boy had opened fire. “I was standing in front of the teacher when she was shot,” a shaken seventh grader tells the BBC, near the gates of Debsirin School in Nonthaburi. “She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up.” Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explains how the shooter stalked from room to room. Authorities say he killed five teachers and injured more than 30 people – including fellow pupils – before turning the weapon on himself. Earlier, he had gunned down his grandparents. “I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends,” the girl, who the BBC is not naming, continues. Her mother says the girl thought she might die. “[She said] ‘I thought I’d never see you again’.” One 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought firecrackers were going off. “I didn’t think it was a gun at first,” he said. “There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again.” Metres from the school gates, paramedics loaded the wounded into ambulances and rushed them to hospital, as milling crowds hugged and cried. Rescue worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith rushed to the scene after hearing children as young as 12 had been hurt. “I saw students who had been shot, some in the arm, some in the back, some in the chest. So I rushed to help get them to the hospital first,” the 47-year-old rescue worker told Reuters news agency. One grieving teacher told the BBC his friend was among the dead. “She was my age. We went to this school together as students. Then we both became teachers at this school,” the 31-year-old, who declined to give his name, said. It is early days in the investigation and police haven’t said anything about a motive. They believe the 9mm handgun the shooter used belonged to his grandfather. Forensic officers found the gunman’s shots to be “quite accurate”, with several hitting “vital spots” on victims’ bodies. Others are filling some of the gaps. A teacher at the school has said the shooter was a good student – not aggressive and with good grades – and education authorities have described him as an avid gamer. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said study pressures may have played a role. “We learned that his grandmother was a teacher and she might have been strict with him. From what the police gathered from his close friend, they knew he was quite stressed about it.” It is clear authorities will have many questions to answer in the coming days – many of them about what change this crime must trigger. Renewed calls for gun control reform This is Thailand’s deadliest mass shooting in years – and the second at a school this year. In February, a head teacher and a female student were shot by an 18-year-old gunman during a school siege in southern Thailand. Four years ago, a 34-year-old in the eastern Nong Bua Lamphu province killed 37 people, most of them preschoolers, in a shooting and stabbing at a nursery. These crimes have resurfaced questions about gun control in the country. “This shouldn’t have happened,” the boyfriend of one of the killed teachers told reporters, clearly distressed and trying to hold back tears. More than seven million people are believed to own guns in the country, one of the highest rates of ownership in the world. Of those, more than one million are unlicensed owners. While there are restrictions on gun licences in Thailand, people can still acquire the weapons – legally or illegally – with relative ease. There is a thriving black market, aided by Thailand’s porous land borders with four other nations. Problems with corruption and loose regulation in the police and military have seen weapons end up in the wrong hands. Prime Minister Anutin said he had tightened regulations when he was interior minister three years ago – suspending new gun permits. But gun crime remains rife, with deaths from gunshots among the highest in the region. And some in the community are calling for greater action. “An act of violence in an educational institution, which should be one of the safest places in our society, serves as a stark reminder for Thai society to seriously and systematically review gun control measures,” Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut, leader of the People’s Party – an opposition party – wrote in a Facebook post.

items.title: Matoto : un incendie réduit en cendres plusieurs commerces au grand marché
items.description: Les commerçants du grand marché de Matoto ont vécu une soirée de désolation ce jeudi 6 août 2026. Un incendie s’est déclaré dans l’enceinte du marché, détruisant plusieurs boutiques et occasionnant d’importantes pertes matérielles. L’origine du sinistre n’était pas encore connue au moment où nous mettions sous presse. Selon des témoins, les flammes se sont propagées rapidement d’un commerce à un autre, laissant peu de temps aux occupants pour sauver leurs marchandises. L’intervention des sapeurs-pompiers, épaulés par des jeunes du quartier, a permis de circonscrire le feu avant qu’il n’atteigne d’autres espaces commerciaux. Pour les victimes, le choc est immense. Certaines affirment avoir perdu en quelques minutes le fruit de plusieurs années de travail. Martine Condé, commerçante spécialisée dans la vente de poisson, explique que son stock venait d’être renouvelé avant le drame. « J’avais rempli mes congélateurs aujourd’hui. Une grande quantité de poisson a été consumée par les flammes. Les pertes sont énormes », témoigne-t-elle, encore sous le coup de l’émotion. Au-delà des dégâts enregistrés, cet incendie remet sur la table la question des conditions d’aménagement du marché. Pour Mamouna Baldé, couturière installée sur les lieux, l’étroitesse des passages a compliqué le travail des équipes de secours. Elle estime qu’une réorganisation des espaces commerciaux est devenue indispensable afin de permettre des interventions plus rapides en cas d’urgence. Ce nouvel incident vient s’ajouter à une série d’incendies enregistrés ces dernières années dans ce centre. Les commerçants invitent les autorités à renforcer les mesures de prévention, à améliorer les infrastructures et à envisager un accompagnement des sinistrés afin de leur permettre de relancer leurs activités.

items.title: Caméras sur 200 km le long de la frontière libyenne avec la Tunisie
items.description: La Garde-frontière libyenne, qui relève du ministère de l’Intérieur du Gouvernement d’unité nationale de Tripoli, a lancé la première phase d’un projet de surveillance électronique destiné à couvrir environ 200 kilomètres de la frontière occidentale de la Libye, le long de la frontière avec la Tunisie. Est-ce que cela va se traduire par une baisse des flux de migrants illégaux subsahariens vers la Tunisie ? On attendra pour voir si ce machin, entre les mains des gardes frontières libyens, va servir à cela ou… à autre chose de plus inavouable. Cette initiative, communiquée par la Garde-frontière libyenne sur sa page Facebook officielle et relayée par le ministère libyen de l’Intérieur, est menée en collaboration avec la mission de l’Union européenne (UE) d’assistance à la gestion intégrée des frontières en Libye (Eubam), précise l’agence italienne Ansa, ajoutant qu’une délégation conjointe s’est rendue dans le secteur frontalier d’Al-Assa, dans la partie nord de la frontière libyo-tunisienne, pour vérifier la mise en œuvre des travaux prévus dans le cadre de cette première phase. Le projet comprend l’installation d’un système de surveillance optique et thermique reposant sur des caméras et des technologies de pointe, conçu pour surveiller la zone frontalière 24 heures sur 24, de jour comme de nuit. Selon la Garde-frontière libyenne, ces équipements devraient améliorer les capacités d’observation et de détection précoce des menaces, tout en renforçant la préparation opérationnelle des unités déployées dans la zone. Ce système vise également à soutenir la lutte contre la contrebande, la migration irrégulière et la criminalité transfrontalière. La coopération dans la zone d’Al-Assa avait déjà été identifiée comme prioritaire en 2024, lors de la première réunion du comité conjoint entre les autorités libyennes et l’Eubam. Les parties avaient convenu de concentrer une première phase d’interventions sur le renforcement des capacités libyennes à Al-Assa et au poste-frontière de Ras Jedir, principal point de passage terrestre entre la Libye et la Tunisie. Eubam est une mission civile de l’UE chargée d’aider les autorités libyennes à gérer les frontières terrestres, maritimes et aériennes, ainsi qu’à lutter contre la traite des êtres humains, le trafic de migrants, la criminalité transfrontalière et le terrorisme. Son mandat actuel a été prorogé jusqu’en juin 2027. I. B. L’article Caméras sur 200 km le long de la frontière libyenne avec la Tunisie est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Burkina: 18 événements culturels et festifs jugés contraires aux bonnes mœurs
items.description: Dans le cadre d'une campagne d'assainissement du secteur culturel, le ministère burkinabè de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme (MCCAT) a ordonné la suspension de 18 manifestations à caractère culturel et récréatif, estimant qu'elles sont contraires aux bonnes mœurs, à l'ordre public et aux valeurs culturelles promues par la Révolution progressiste populaire. L'information a été rapportée, ce vendredi 7 août 2026, par l'Agence d'information du Burkina (AIB). Le ministère burkinabè de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme (MCCAT) a engagé une nouvelle étape de sa campagne d'assainissement du secteur culturel en mettant en demeure plusieurs promoteurs de manifestations festives de suspendre leurs activités. Selon l'Agence d'information du Burkina (AIB), les autorités estiment que ces événements sont susceptibles de porter atteinte à la moralité publique, à l'ordre public, aux bonnes mœurs ainsi qu'à la protection des mineurs. D'après les informations rapportées, dix-huit événements sont concernés par cette décision. Il s'agit notamment de «The Out Side à Loumbila», «Golden Moment à Ouaga 2000», «Young Day», «Tropical Summer», «Ouaga Show Piscine Party», «Happy Run Blue Ouaga», «The Chill and Barbecue», «Afro Trap-Crazy», «All White Party», «Urban Vibes à Bobo-Dioulasso», «Ouaga Summer», «Sun and Fun-Kam City», «Ouaga Plage», «Top Vacances», «Infinity Moment», «Ouaga Fiesta», «Ouaga Vibes et Festy Luchas», organisés par différents promoteurs. Le ministère prévient que tout manquement à cette mise en demeure pourrait entraîner des mesures administratives visant à faire cesser les activités concernées, en plus des sanctions prévues par la réglementation en vigueur. Ces sanctions peuvent aller de l'avertissement au retrait de l'autorisation d'exercer, en passant par des amendes, voire l'interdiction d'exercer une activité artistique ou assimilée. Cette opération s'inscrit dans l'application de la loi n°004-2025/ALT du 27 mars 2025 portant statut de l'artiste au Burkina Faso. Ce texte précise notamment que la création, la reproduction, la diffusion et la distribution des œuvres artistiques doivent être conformes aux lois et règlements en vigueur. Il impose également aux artistes professionnels de détenir une autorisation délivrée par le ministère chargé des Arts et interdit toute création ou promotion d'activités portant atteinte à l'ordre public et aux bonnes mœurs. C'est une décision qui intervient au lendemain d'une mesure similaire visant l'artiste Kosa Pic. Celui-ci a été sommé de retirer des publications liées à sa récente création artistique, également considérées comme contraires aux bonnes mœurs. À travers cette série de mises en demeure, les autorités burkinabè affichent leur volonté de renforcer l'encadrement des activités artistiques et culturelles en s'appuyant sur les dispositions du statut de l'artiste. Selon l'Agence d'information du Burkina (AIB), cette campagne d'assainissement devrait se poursuivre afin de promouvoir des manifestations conformes aux exigences légales, aux règles d'éthique et aux valeurs culturelles défendues par les pouvoirs publics. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Burkina: 18 événements culturels et festifs jugés contraires aux bonnes mœurs est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: The Dishonesty of True Crime
items.description: On October 9, 2020, Taylor Parker, a 27-year-old mother of two, visited her friend Reagan Simmons-Hancock at her home in northeastern Texas. Simmons-Hancock, who was 35 weeks pregnant with her second child, had something Parker felt she desperately needed: a baby. What transpired next is the subject of Maternal Instinct , a hit Netflix true-crime documentary directed by Jessica Dimmock and released in June. If you watched the film, you might conclude that you know everything you need to know about Parker and her crimes. But you would be mistaken. What is remarkable—albeit in line with the demands of the true-crime genre—is just how much Maternal Instinct leaves out. True-crime documentaries are entertainment. They tend to follow a formula with common elements: villains and victims, mystery and suspense, capture and catharsis. These stories typically adopt the tropes of horror films—eerie music, ominous foreshadowing—and offer the prosecution’s version of events, which favor a tidy and dramatic view of a killer’s means and motives. The defense’s job is to poke holes in these assumptions. By omitting vital details from defense teams—in Parker’s case and others—true-crime films portray the grisliest offenses as essentially incomprehensible expressions of wickedness, when the reality is invariably more complicated. The documentary opens with an acquaintance of Parker’s observing that “there’s evil in our land” and that “evil people do evil things.” This is more of a spiritual explanation than a legal or clinical one. No one can know the fundamental character of another person’s soul, but Maternal Instinct hardly tries to understand Parker’s. Parker is clearly guilty of committing two horrifying murders. Her evident mental illness does, however, challenge the claim that her actions could be explained only by inveterate evil. [ McKay Coppins: The gross spectacle of murder fandom ] As Maternal Instinct recounts, in the months prior to that October morning in Simmons-Hancock’s home, Parker, a divorced mother of two, had staged a fake pregnancy. She had gone to great lengths to convince the people around her—including her fairly new boyfriend—that she was expecting. She’d padded her belly, fabricated medical documents and ultrasounds, and claimed that coronavirus-pandemic restrictions mandated that she see her doctors solo. But unbeknownst to her boyfriend and others, Parker was infertile, having undergone a hysterectomy years earlier. To keep her lies from being exposed, Parker sought a newborn child to make her own. According to police, she arrived at the house of her very pregnant friend with a scalpel and bludgeoned the 21-year-old Simmons-Hancock with what was likely a hammer, then wrestled her to the floor, sliced her uterus open, and extracted her unborn child. Parker then fled the scene with the infant, leaving Simmons-Hancock to die; the infant died later that day. In 2022, after two years in prison and a weekslong trial, Parker was found guilty of capital murder by a Texas jury and sentenced to death. Maternal Instinct is meant to paint a portrait of a criminal and her crime, but Parker, who remains on death row, was neither interviewed nor consulted for the documentary—nor were her defense attorneys or their expert witnesses, though Dimmock and her team offered them a chance to comment before releasing the film. Dimmock explained to me that she’d declined to interview Parker out of respect for Simmons-Hancock’s family and friends, and because she doubted that Parker would be truthful or remorseful. True-crime stories about female killers tend to be especially titillating. Men are about nine times more likely to commit murder than women—who are assumed to be, as the Cornell Law School professor Sandra Babcock put it, “peaceful, nurturing, mothering, caring, obedient.” Murder “seems so out of step with how we view women, how we perceive the stereotypical woman as being,” Babcock, who specializes in gender rights and the death penalty, told me. Parker’s trial gave rise to a profusion of lurid headlines: “Texas Woman Allegedly Stabbed Mom-to-Be 100 Times, Then Tried to Steal Baby from Womb,” reported People magazine; “Neurologist: Taylor Parker’s Brain Is ‘Broken;’ Defense Rests,” offered the local NBC affiliate KTAL News. Body-cam clips of Parker’s interactions with police spread on YouTube and TikTok. The coverage inspired Maternal Instinct and sets its tone; Dimmock told me that much of her team’s preliminary research into Parker’s case came from the news articles and video clips disseminated online. Maternal Instinct includes interviews with Parker’s former friends and acquaintances, who describe the broad scope of Parker’s lies over the years, including her many allegedly fictitious ailments and her claims that she was due to receive a multimillion-dollar inheritance from her oil-baron grandparents, who were, in reality, of no particular means. To maintain her deceptions about the pregnancy and other matters, Parker owned multiple cellphones for sending fraudulent messages, fabricated official letters, and used voice-altering software to place anonymous calls. Randi Chavez, an investigator brought on by Parker’s attorneys, met with Parker for hundreds of hours over the course of a year. Chavez retained experts to assess Parker’s mental and neurological health, and she interviewed people who knew her, including relatives and fellow prisoners. What she discovered was that Parker had displayed symptoms of profound mental illness for many years. To stipulate that Parker’s mental illness played a significant role in her ghastly crimes is not to suggest that she should have been found either incompetent to stand trial or not guilty by reason of insanity, both of which are exceedingly rare outcomes. Her defense instead presented evidence of her mental illness as a factor that ought to have spared her from the death penalty, but not from punishment altogether. (The American Psychiatric Association, the American Bar Association, and other professional groups have called for a ban on the death penal­ty for those with severe mental illness.) Yet like Parker’s jury, Maternal Instinct does not take Parker to be seriously mentally ill. At Parker’s trial, the prosecution called upon the forensic psychiatrist Michael Arambula to testify that Parker showed signs of borderline personality disorder, a condition marked by intense mood swings, unstable relationships, impulsivity, fear of abandonment, and feelings of emptiness. But Arambula’s testimony undermined the seriousness of the illness by likening it to intentionally malicious behavior. Borderline personality disorder, he told the jury, is “probably the most manipulative of the personality types.” Parker, he said, had a “pleasant and engaging demeanor atop a core of rage.” He denied that mental illness had contributed to Parker’s murders, insisting to the jury that the uncommon brutality of her crimes did not mean that she was delusional. Members of Simmons-Hancock’s family have likewise adamantly maintained that Parker is “evil” rather than “crazy.” [ Megan Garber: America’s constant need for entertainment has blurred the line between fiction and reality ] But Arambula delivered his testimony without ever meeting or interviewing Parker. He drew his conclusions from a review of Parker’s medical records. The defense’s mental-health experts, who’d actually met Parker, came to very different conclusions. At trial, the defense called a psychiatrist, a neurologist, and a social worker, all of whom confirmed that Parker suffered from a personality disorder that was exacerbated by a personal history of trauma and abuse. They found that Parker’s teenage mother had been negligent, disengaged, and hostile to her daughter before abandoning the family when Parker was a teenager. Her father, meanwhile, had abused methamphetamines, and when Parker was 12, he’d taken her to a house frequented by drug users, where, she said, a man raped her. Maternal Instinct neither reported nor probed those allegations. After Parker’s conviction, lawyers working on her appeals invited more experts to expand this evidence. Nicole Anders, a clinical psychologist for the defense who met with Parker in January 2025, confirmed that Parker displayed traits associated with borderline personality disorder and argued that this condition—which Anders discussed in the context of Parker’s history of trauma and abuse—significantly altered her ability to reason or function. In a declaration submitted to the court, Anders stated that the trauma and sexual abuse Parker endured as a child had left her hypervigilant, prone to delusion, and desperate for emotional connection. “Although these coping strategies may be maladaptive in the long term,” Anders wrote in her clinical report, “they are rooted in survival instincts. When safe, consistent caregiving is absent or unpredictable early in life, the nervous system adapts to prioritize protection over connection or reason.” Craig Malkin, a lecturer in psychology at Harvard Medical School, told me that personality disorders form when a patient’s ways of coping with traumatic experiences become deeply ingrained. “We all develop some kind of psychological armor,” Malkin said, which “are just ways of protecting ourselves in vulnerable moments when we’re ashamed, when we fear rejection, when we’re sad and helpless.” For Parker, coping with her mother’s rejection, her father’s destructive irresponsibility, and her own desolate loneliness meant developing delusional fantasies and resorting to extreme people-pleasing behavior. Winning the affection of others sometimes meant lying to them about what she had to offer. Borderline patients, Malkin said, “are people who live on the edge of neurosis and psychosis,” meaning that they alternate between struggling to solve everyday problems and losing touch with reality altogether. According to experts who spoke with Parker during and after her trial, those delusions centered on her fertility. In 2014, six years before the murders, Parker sought a routine tubal ligation to prevent further pregnancies, but the procedure failed. When a gynecologist confirmed to Parker a year later that she was pregnant, Parker was relieved. She concluded that it was a sign from God that she was meant to have another child. But during a subsequent surgery to remove a cyst on her right ovary, her doctor discovered that the pregnancy was ectopic and developing in her left fallopian tube. While Parker was still under anesthesia, her surgical team procured consent from her then-husband to undertake a total abdominal hysterectomy, removing Parker’s fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and right ovary. Although Maternal Instinct notes that Parker’s hysterectomy left her unable to have children, the film neglects to mention how it happened or how she felt about it. Parker was shattered when she awoke to find that she could no longer bear children. She confided in friends at the time and later told Diana Barnes, a women’s-mental-health expert brought in by her defense team, that she felt robbed of her identity and purpose in life. She became fixated on pregnancy and childbirth, took a job at a women’s health clinic to be near babies, spent her free time watching mothers and children at parks and stores, and desperately researched surrogacy and uterine transplants, even soliciting her mother for her uterus. As Parker’s obsession progressed, her marriage broke down, and her mental health unraveled. She told others that she had again become pregnant and miscarried, though that was not possible. She told Barnes that when she placed a mock pregnancy belly on her body in 2020, she felt as though it were really her flesh. Parker was clearly unwell in the months and years leading up to the murders, a fact that Maternal Instinct elides. The documentary suggests that Parker’s crimes were carefully calculated out of selfishness and deceit: A malevolent young woman conspired to entrap her boyfriend with a fake pregnancy and needed a newborn to pull off the plot, so she brutally murdered a friend and stole her baby. But that version of events raises questions that can be answered only by Parker’s mental illness: Why was her desire for love and acceptance so overwhelming that it curdled into criminality? What made the prospect of having a baby with her boyfriend seem worth killing for? Suggesting that Parker’s evil nature alone explains her many schemes and lies is both reductive and unsatisfying. The film does not explain how someone so adept at weaving elaborate falsehoods might fail to anticipate that staff at the hospital where she arrived with Simmons-Hancock’s baby would also inquire into her own condition. People who had doubted her pregnancy were bound to notice that Simmons-Hancock’s murder and Parker’s “birth” had coincided. But Parker was not thinking clearly, and had not been for some time. [ Atlantic documentaries: America is obsessed with serial killers ] Murder is, after all, not a good idea. Some people commit murder without having thought it through at all, but that sort of crime does not make one eligible for the death penalty. Murders that are eligible for the death penalty involve some degree of premeditation and intent. The presence of planning is usually taken to be proof that a murderer had a sober appreciation for what they meant to do, but it also suggests that something was seriously wrong with their capacity to reason; otherwise, they would have come to the conclusion that, whatever their predicament, murder could only compound it. This does not seem to have occurred to Taylor Parker. The origins of many murders eligible for the death penalty seem to lie less in deeply rooted inherent wickedness than in particularly compromised minds. Such nuance is usually absent from true-crime yarns, however, because acknowledging mental illness and other impairments complicates simplistic narratives. The genre captivates audiences by dramatizing the worst human behavior, but these stories almost always neglect to illuminate the whole truth, which is stranger and more tragic than what passes for good TV.

items.title: Bring Back the Blue-Book Exam
items.description: Across the faded blue covers of the exam books in my attic, I can trace the arc of my academic career. I can still see the grades I received on tests in “The Meaning of Abstraction in Modern Art” (A) and in Neurobiology (B–). Just the sight of the booklets is enough for me to feel the pressure to perform, to sculpt the contents of a semester’s worth of knowledge into some fresh shape. But by the time I became a college professor myself, in 2013, the blue book had begun to disappear. Why struggle to discern student penmanship, or risk misplacing a final exam in the trunk of one’s Subaru (to cite a completely hypothetical example), when tests, like everything else, can be administered on a laptop? The coronavirus made every aspect of education virtual, but even after it abated, in-person final exams remained out of favor for many classes. Part of the reason was simply administrative—the challenge of finding faculty or graduate students to watch over the test-takers. But there was also a shift in how teachers appraised student learning . The blue book meant timed essays and handwritten work, modes of assessment that felt regressive, cruel. It recalled an age of higher education—punitive and bleak, the domain of Dickens’s stern Mr. Gradgrind—that the modern university was eager to outgrow. Not entirely, of course; some faculty still lugged boxes of blue books home in the snow and scribbled grades in red on the covers. But alternatives to the in-person exam proliferated: the capstone project, the take-home essay, the portfolio of selected work from the semester. The blue book seemed destined to become a relic , as obsolete as cursive. But it had one virtue that hasn’t been easy to replicate: Cheating on a blue-book exam is difficult. When faculty moved away from in-person pen-and-paper exams, they assumed that cheating would be kept in check by honor codes, or by “locked” browsers, which would prevent students from accessing sites that would jog their memory or simply give them the answers. But these measures were never wholly effective. In a survey of undergraduates published in 2020 , 62 percent admitted to cheating in some manner. The advent of AI has only exacerbated the problem. In a matter of seconds, students can create an entire essay with the help of a chatbot. If they’re savvy, they can spend a bit more time to make it sound authentically human enough to evade detection by their professor. As my colleague Rose Horowitch has reported, such cheating has become so prevalent that Princeton recently gave up on its venerable honor code . For 133 years, students had signed a pledge not to cheat, and professors had trusted them to do the right thing. In May, in the face of rampant AI-enabled cheating, the university’s faculty voted to begin proctoring exams for the first time since the Gilded Age. [ Rose Horowitch: How AI killed a 133-year-old Princeton tradition ] Universities find themselves in a surprising position. The only reliable way to evaluate what students have learned may be to bring back pen and paper. Faculty are reverting to in-person, handwritten assignments and timed essays—anything that keeps assessments offline. The unlikely hero of the day is the blue book, sales of which are up by as much as 80 percent for some universities since 2023. Yet the blue book is more than a last redoubt against cheating. Despite its antiquated appearance, the blue book encourages experimentation, even virtuosity. It deserves to live on not because of what it rejects but because of what it makes possible: thinking on the page, a hallmark of the humanities that is indispensable to their value—and essential to the kinds of human beings that a liberal-arts institution hopes to send out into the world. The blue book hasn’t changed much for a hundred years or more, with its sky-blue tint and pale-red margin lines, its two neat staples and wide-open spacing, and its austere list of requirements on the cover ( NAME, SUBJECT, CLASS, SECTION ). The precise history of the blue book is lost to time. One origin story pinpoints its emergence in the 1920s at Butler University; the pamphlet is said to have borrowed its distinctive hue from the university’s colors. Harvard lore suggests that the blue book is older still: By one account, a classics instructor, Evangelinus Apostolides Sophocles, burned a stack of blue-book exams to protest the university’s move from oral to written examinations in 1857. I realize that by advocating for the blue book in 2026, I might be engaging in the same opposition to progress as old Professor Sophocles. But to me, the blue book represents a timeless human activity—namely, trusting your mind to discover unknown capabilities . [ Walt Hunter: Stop meeting students where they are ] I think of my college-age self, looking up at the clock as I turned the page, crossed out a sentence, broke the tip of my pencil. I recall the satisfaction of filling one book and getting up from my desk to take another, the adrenaline of using my knowledge to improvise something and then having more to say. What I learned by writing this way was distinct from what I learned by composing a five-paragraph essay, with its thesis statement, staid structure, and rote deployment of argument and evidence. Any AI agent can mimic that template. Taking a blue-book exam is an almost athletic endeavor, and not just because of the stamina it requires of both mind and hand. The test-taker is forced to compose an essay that will demonstrate their command of a semester’s or year’s worth of material. They have to summon the verve to tackle a prompt about the place of freedom in the American novel, or the value of a human life in Hamlet , or what Whitman meant when he said that “ the United States themselves are essentially the greatest poem .” Staring down the empty pages of a blue book, I learned to throw myself into my writing. In the process, I discovered what I was capable of as a writer and a thinker. When you’ve done the reading and reviewed your lecture notes, you can feel like a basketball player whose hours in the gym made possible a transcendent playoff performance, or like a musician whose endless runs of arpeggios in a soundproof practice room allowed for a spectacular solo in the concert hall. Not every student can put pencil to paper for 90 minutes without looking up. Even the strongest students can struggle, at first, to answer the question, or to organize their thoughts. But this, too, is a reason to love the blue book. When students write, they write into uncertainty. They court risk. No surrogate exists for feeling an idea form in your mind and trying to express that idea on the page. And wonderfully, for the instructor, the blue book documents how students strain their way to an answer or an argument. The marks on the page are indelible, and efforts to amend them leave marks of their own: furious erasing or hasty strike-throughs. The blue book is a record of first thoughts, instincts, intuitions. These fits and starts and failed experiments are a good thing—for the education of the individual and for the health of a society. The humanities are distinguished by the habits of mind that they inculcate , not for their success in forcing students to memorize facts. Among the most significant of these habits are a nimbleness of thought and a flexibility of argument, the ability to draw connections between diverse sets of facts. Those habits are honed by writing under pressure. Challenged by the blue book, students learn to identify and stand behind their individual commitments. As their professor, I hope they carry that lesson beyond the classroom, beyond the university, and into the fractious world they enter as citizens. [ From the July/August 2023 issue: A defense of humanity in the age of AI ] Often the key insight arrives just as time is expiring, and I love how no part of the book is out of bounds for a final thought at the buzzer. “Education is the single greatest thing Thoreau believes in,” one student sneaks into the margins of the final for my American-literature course. For the teacher, this is the pleasure of the blue book—despite its uniform presentation and its rigid lineation, any part of it might reveal a sudden moonshot of an idea. Many of the best sentences appear on the back inside cover, such as this ending to an essay on Toni Morrison: “A good life is what we make it to be—now all we have to do is live it.” Students, of course, know what they’ve been taught: the timeline of the English Civil War, the structure of a sonnet by Gwendolyn Brooks, the development of a motif in a Mahler symphony. But the blue book demands more than a recitation of facts. It asks students to demonstrate not just that they know when or where something happened, but why it did. It asks them not just who wrote a poem, or when, but what the poem conveys about the world in which it was written. The best-prepared students, the ones who inhabit the history and poetry and music that have made up the semester’s syllabus, find that they understand the material in ways they didn’t appreciate before they opened the blue book and the clock started ticking. Proponents of artificial intelligence have promised that, by removing certain elements of the craft of writing, students can concentrate on making their work more polished and their ideas more clearly defined. That’s a dangerous ruse. To see what a student has learned, look at the moment when they struggle to begin—and then transcend that struggle to create something genuinely surprising. That’s the moment the full force of the writer’s mind takes possession of the process. When we eliminate the possibility of writing badly or incoherently, we eliminate writing’s greatest satisfaction: the feeling that we have stepped outside ourselves and are watching our own words fall together in the right order. What I describe sounds like a state of grace, but it’s also a furious act of intellection and expression undertaken with only one’s study and wits to guide them. I’ve come to love handing out blue books on exam day and seeing the look of ready intelligence on my students’ faces. The essay they are about to write will be better than they think it can be. All they have to do is write it. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “The Blue Book Is Back.”

items.title: 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations Unies : le Sénégalais Djibril Diallo nommé chef de cabinet du Président
items.description: Le Dr Djibril Diallo, haut fonctionnaire international sénégalais, a été nommé chef de cabinet de S.E. M. Khalilur Rahman, président de la 81e session de l'Assemblée générale des Nations Unies, élu le 02 juin 2026. Cette nomination place une personnalité sénégalaise de grande expérience au cœur de la diplomatie mondiale, à un moment particulièrement important pour l'avenir des Nations Unies et du multilatéralisme. Selon le communiqué qui donne l'information, Dr Diallo rejoindra prochainement New York pour prendre ses fonctions. Il accompagnera le président Rahman dans la mise en œuvre de ses priorités, la coordination des travaux de son Bureau et le dialogue avec les 193 États membres, le secrétaire général et l'ensemble du système des Nations Unies. Le document renseigne que la 81e session sera notamment marquée par la sélection et la nomination d'un nouveau secrétaire général des Nations Unies. Et parmi les candidats figure Macky Sall, ancien président de la République du Sénégal. Elle s'ouvrira également dans un contexte de crises internationales majeures et de débats sur la réforme de l'organisation. Pour le Dr Djibril Diallo, cette nomination représente un retour au cœur d'une institution qu'il connaît particulièrement bien pour y avoir déjà exercé les fonctions de porte-parole du Président de l'Assemblée générale et de conseiller principal auprès de plusieurs de ses présidents. Cette nomination couronne un parcours de plus de trente-cinq ans au sein du système des Nations Unies où il a eu à assumer d'importantes responsabilités à l'Onusida, au Pnud, à l'Unicef et au Haut-Commissariat des Nations Unies pour les réfugiés. Dr Diallo a également dirigé, à New York, le Bureau des Nations Unies pour le sport au service du développement et de la paix. Originaire de Kolda, Dr Djibril Diallo a effectué ses études secondaires à Ziguinchor avant d'obtenir son premier diplôme universitaire à l'Université Cheikh Anta Diop de Dakar. Il a ensuite poursuivi ses études au Royaume-Uni, où il a obtenu un doctorat de l'Université de Londres. Sa nomination constitue donc une nouvelle reconnaissance de l'expertise sénégalaise sur la scène internationale. La 81e session de l'Assemblée générale des Nations Unies s'ouvrira le 8 septembre 2026 au siège de l'ONU à New York. Ndiol Maka SECK

items.title: CAF : Samuel Eto'o blanchi en appel dans l'affaire du match face au Maroc
items.description: La Commission d'appel de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF) a annulé l'ensemble des sanctions infligées à Samuel Eto'o, président de la Fédération camerounaise de football (Fecafoot), dans le dossier lié au match entre le Cameroun et le Maroc lors de la CAN 2025. Dans un communiqué, la Fecafoot a indiqué que la décision, rendue le 5 août 2026, annule toutes les sanctions prononcées précédemment ainsi que leurs effets juridiques. L'affaire concernait la rencontre opposant le Cameroun au Maroc le 9 janvier 2026, dans le cadre de la Coupe d'Afrique des nations « Maroc 2025 ». À l'issue de cette rencontre, la Commission disciplinaire de la CAF avait estimé que Samuel Eto'o avait enfreint les principes d'intégrité, de loyauté et d'esprit sportif prévus par les statuts et le Code disciplinaire de l'instance. En première instance, l'ancien capitaine des Lions Indomptables avait été sanctionné d'une interdiction d'accès aux stades pour les quatre prochains matches officiels de la CAN, ainsi que d'une amende de 20 000 dollars. Saisie du dossier, la Commission d'appel a finalement décidé d'annuler ces sanctions. La Fédération camerounaise de football s'est félicitée de cette décision, estimant qu'elle illustre l'indépendance des organes judiciaires de la CAF et leur volonté d'appliquer le droit de manière objective et équitable. La Fecafoot a également réaffirmé sa confiance dans les instances juridictionnelles de la Confédération africaine, saluant leur engagement en faveur du respect des principes de légalité et d'une justice sportive indépendante, au service de la crédibilité du football africain. The post CAF : Samuel Eto'o blanchi en appel dans l'affaire du match face au Maroc appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Un essai à « guillotine » contre la négation démocratique en Afrique
items.description: Dans un contexte marqué par la multiplication des coups d’État, la montée des discours souverainistes et la remise en cause du modèle démocratique libéral, Ousmane Ndiaye publie « L’Afrique contre la démocratie. Mythes, déni et péril ». L’essai s’attache à démonter les récits qui, selon son auteur, ont progressivement installé une lecture déformée de son histoire politique. Le titre peut surprendre. À première vue, « L’Afrique contre la démocratie » laisse croire à une dénonciation d’un continent réfractaire aux principes démocratiques. Il n’en est rien. Le véritable objet du livre est ailleurs. Ousmane Ndiaye montre que ce sont moins les sociétés africaines qui se sont détournées de la démocratie que les récits produits autour d’elles qui ont fini par brouiller la compréhension de leur histoire politique. L’ouvrage s’inscrit dans un moment particulier de l’histoire politique africaine. Depuis plusieurs années, les transitions militaires au Mali, au Burkina Faso, au Niger ou encore en Guinée alimentent un discours selon lequel la démocratie serait un modèle en échec, incapable de répondre aux attentes des populations. À cette crise institutionnelle s’ajoute une bataille des idées dans laquelle les réseaux sociaux, certains intellectuels et une partie des acteurs politiques contribuent à opposer démocratie, souveraineté et aspirations populaires. C’est précisément cette bataille des récits qu’Ousmane Ndiaye choisit d’explorer. Son ambition est de questionner les évidences qui se sont imposées dans le débat public. Son point de départ est que nombre de certitudes sur la démocratie en Afrique reposent moins sur les faits que sur des constructions idéologiques répétées jusqu’à acquérir le statut de vérité. La première cible est le discours de La Baule. Depuis plus de trois décennies, le sommet franco-africain de 1990 est souvent présenté comme l’acte fondateur des transitions démocratiques africaines. L’auteur démonte cette lecture en rappelant que les mobilisations populaires, les revendications démocratiques et même certaines conférences nationales avaient commencé avant l’intervention de François Mitterrand. Selon lui, attribuer à la France l’origine de la démocratisation du continent revient à invisibiliser les luttes menées par les Africains eux-mêmes. Cette démonstration constitue l’une des parties les plus convaincantes du livre. En replaçant les événements dans leur chronologie, l’auteur rappelle utilement que les transformations politiques ne surgissent jamais d’un discours présidentiel, mais d’un long processus social et politique. La Baule apparaît ainsi davantage comme une tentative de récupération diplomatique que comme un véritable point de départ historique. À partir de cette relecture, Ousmane Ndiaye développe une idée plus large. Une déconstruction épistémique Les années 1990 auraient moins consacré la démocratie qu’elles n’auraient favorisé l’installation de ce qu’il appelle des « fictions démocratiques ». Les partis uniques ont disparu, les élections se sont multipliées, mais les mécanismes de confiscation du pouvoir sont, selon lui, restés largement inchangés. Plusieurs États ont adopté les codes du pluralisme sans modifier en profondeur leurs pratiques de gouvernement. Cette critique, désormais largement documentée par les travaux sur les démocraties hybrides, trouve ici une formulation accessible et solidement argumentée. L’auteur s’attaque ensuite à un autre récit devenu dominant, celui qui présente les régimes militaires comme une solution aux échecs des pouvoirs civils. Il refuse ce qu’il nomme le faux clivage entre civils et militaires. Selon lui, l’histoire politique du continent montre, au contraire, que les armées ont souvent été des acteurs centraux des systèmes de pouvoir. Elles ont participé à leur consolidation, à leur maintien ou à leur renversement. Les présenter aujourd’hui comme une alternative extérieure au politique relève, à ses yeux, d’une lecture sélective de l’histoire. L’analyse du Mali illustre cette démonstration. Ousmane Ndiaye rappelle que le coup d’État d’Assimi Goïta intervient dans un contexte de contestation populaire déjà très avancé, porté notamment par le mouvement M5-Rfp. Le pouvoir militaire n’apparaît donc pas comme l’origine de la rupture politique, mais comme l’aboutissement d’une crise dont les racines sont d’abord civiles. Cette mise en perspective permet de nuancer les lectures simplificatrices qui réduisent les transitions actuelles à une opposition entre militaires vertueux et dirigeants civils défaillants. L’essai prend également ses distances avec une partie du discours panafricaniste contemporain. Sans remettre en cause les aspirations à la souveraineté, l’auteur met en garde contre une rhétorique qui tend parfois à faire de l’autoritarisme un prix acceptable de l’indépendance politique. Il souligne que le rejet de l’influence occidentale ne peut constituer, à lui seul, un projet démocratique. La souveraineté, insiste-t-il, ne dispense ni de la séparation des pouvoirs, ni des libertés publiques, ni du contrôle citoyen. C’est sans doute dans cette volonté de réintroduire de la complexité que réside la principale force de l’ouvrage. Ousmane Ndiaye refuse les oppositions binaires : démocratie contre souveraineté, civils contre militaires, Afrique contre Occident. Il montre que ces catégories, souvent mobilisées dans le débat public, masquent des réalités historiques plus nuancées. L’auteur avance également une proposition de reconstruction. Il plaide pour une réflexion sur les institutions qui prenne davantage appui sur les expériences politiques africaines. Il mobilise notamment l’exemple du « Naxlé » dans les sociétés léboues, pour montrer que les principes de responsabilité collective, de délibération et de partage de l’espace public existaient bien avant l’importation des modèles constitutionnels contemporains. Son propos ne consiste pas à opposer une démocratie africaine à une démocratie occidentale. Il affirme, au contraire, que les valeurs démocratiques sont universelles, mais que leur enracinement passe nécessairement par l’histoire et les pratiques sociales de chaque société. Par Amadou KÉBÉ

items.title: Trump : de Superman à la mouche du coche
items.description: Après plusieurs mois de conflit, le détroit d'Ormuz devrait prochainement rouvrir à la circulation maritime.
